summary.text: Assuming the first claimed identity, \(b_k=a_{3773+k}+1\) satisfies the Fibonacci recurrence; a modular Fibonacci computation modulo \(195318521017\) gives \(b_K\equiv b_{K+1}\equiv1\) for \(K=249580073233\), so that modulus divides two consecutive positive terms. Their gcd \(g>1\), and at the next index the defining recurrence and claimed identity would force \(g+s/g=1+s\), where \(s\ge2g\); thus \(s/g\ge2\), contradicting the equivalent equation \((g-1)(s/g-1)=0\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(a_1=a_2=1\), and for \(n\geq 3\) let
\[
 a_n=d_n+\frac{a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}}{d_n},
 \qquad d_n=\gcd(a_{n-1},a_{n-2}).
\]
The quotient is an integer because \(d_n\) divides both summands. We will disprove the conjecture by showing that even its first asserted identity
\[
 a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}\tag{1}
\]
cannot hold for every \(n\geq 3775\). Since the full conjecture asserts (1) together with two further identities for every such \(n\), this suffices to disprove the full conjunction.

All the terms \(a_n\) are positive. Indeed, this is true initially, and if two consecutive terms are positive, then their gcd is positive and hence so is the next term given by the recurrence.

We argue by contradiction. Suppose that (1) holds for every \(n\geq3775\). Introduce the shifted sequence
\[
 c_k=a_{3773+k}+1\qquad(k\geq0).
\]
For every \(k\geq0\), applying (1) at \(n=3775+k\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 c_{k+2}
 &=a_{3775+k}+1\\
 &=\bigl(1+a_{3774+k}+a_{3773+k}\bigr)+1\\
 &=\bigl(a_{3774+k}+1\bigr)+\bigl(a_{3773+k}+1\bigr)\\
 &=c_{k+1}+c_k.
\end{aligned}\tag{2}
\]
Thus, under the conjectural identity, \((c_k)\) must obey the ordinary Fibonacci recurrence from its first two values onward.

Write \(F_0=0,F_1=1\), and \(F_{m+2}=F_{m+1}+F_m\). Equation (2), by a straightforward induction, gives for every \(k\geq1\)
\[
 c_k=c_1F_k+c_0F_{k-1}.\tag{3}
\]
The base case \(k=1\) is
\(c_1=c_1F_1+c_0F_0\). If the formula holds at two consecutive indices, adding those two formulas and using the Fibonacci recurrence proves it at the next index, so (3) follows for all \(k\geq1\).

We now use the following concrete modulus and index:
\[
 p=195318521017,
 \qquad K=249580073233.
\]
No primality property of \(p\) is required.

First, a finite evaluation of the defining recurrence from \((a_1,a_2)=(1,1)\) through indices 3773 and 3774 gives
\[
 a_{3773}\equiv77940394258\pmod p,
 \qquad
 a_{3774}\equiv99768150821\pmod p.\tag{4}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 c_0\equiv77940394259\pmod p,
 \qquad
 c_1\equiv99768150822\pmod p.\tag{5}
\]
For completeness, the finite calculation in (4) is obtained by repeatedly applying the exact integer pair update
\[
 (x,y)\longmapsto
 \left(y,\gcd(x,y)+\frac{x+y}{\gcd(x,y)}\right).
\]
Starting with \((1,1)=(a_1,a_2)\), after \(3772\) updates this produces \((a_{3773},a_{3774})\). The gcd and division are performed on the exact integers at each step, and reducing the two resulting final integers modulo \(195318521017\) gives the two residues in (4). This calculation involves only finitely many applications of the displayed recurrence; the final terms have respectively 340 and 341 decimal digits.

We also need three Fibonacci residues. They are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 F_{K-1}=F_{249580073232}&\equiv117378126758\pmod p,\\
 F_K=F_{249580073233}&\equiv21827756563\pmod p,\\
 F_{K+1}=F_{249580073234}&\equiv139205883321\pmod p.
\end{aligned}\tag{6}
\]
These modular values can be obtained directly by Fibonacci fast doubling. Namely, for any \(m\), from the pair \((F_m,F_{m+1})\) one computes
\[
\begin{aligned}
 F_{2m}&=F_m\bigl(2F_{m+1}-F_m\bigr),\\
 F_{2m+1}&=F_m^2+F_{m+1}^2,\\
 F_{2m+2}&=F_{2m}+F_{2m+1}.
\end{aligned}\tag{7}
\]
All these equations may be reduced modulo \(p\) after each operation. The relevant binary expansions are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 K-1&=(11101000011100001000011011000100010000)_2,\\
 K&=(11101000011100001000011011000100010001)_2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Beginning with \((F_0,F_1)=(0,1)\), reading either binary expansion from left to right and using (7) produces
\[
 (F_{K-1},F_K)\equiv(117378126758,21827756563)\pmod p
\]
and
\[
 (F_K,F_{K+1})\equiv(21827756563,139205883321)\pmod p,
\]
which is exactly (6). Thus (6) is a short modular computation requiring only 38 doubling steps.

Apply the forced formula (3) first at \(k=K\). Using (5) and (6),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 c_K
 &\equiv99768150822\cdot21827756563
   +77940394259\cdot117378126758\pmod p.
\end{aligned}
\]
The integer on the right is
\[
 11326212385784681827108
   =195318521017\cdot57988419771+1.
\]
Therefore
\[
 c_K\equiv1\pmod p.\tag{8}
\]
Similarly, formula (3) at \(k=K+1\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 c_{K+1}
 &\equiv99768150822\cdot139205883321
   +77940394259\cdot21827756563\pmod p.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the integer on the right is
\[
 15589577514788957011679
   =195318521017\cdot79816176334+1,
\]
so
\[
 c_{K+1}\equiv1\pmod p.\tag{9}
\]
By the definition \(c_k=a_{3773+k}+1\), congruences (8) and (9) imply
\[
 p\mid a_{3773+K}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 p\mid a_{3773+K+1}.\tag{10}
\]
In ordinary decimal indices, these are the two consecutive terms
\[
 a_{249580077006}\quad\text{and}\quad a_{249580077007}.
\]

Set
\[
 x=a_{249580077007},\qquad
 y=a_{249580077006},\qquad
 g=\gcd(x,y),\qquad
 s=x+y,
\]
and put \(q=s/g\). By (10), \(p\) divides both \(x\) and \(y\), and hence \(p\mid g\). Since \(p>1\) and \(g>0\), it follows that
\[
 g\geq p>1.\tag{11}
\]
Moreover, \(x,y>0\). Since \(g\mid x\) and \(g\mid y\), each positive integer \(x,y\) is at least \(g\). Therefore
\[
 s=x+y\geq2g,
\]
and hence
\[
 q=\frac{s}{g}\geq2.\tag{12}
\]

Now consider the next index
\[
 N=249580077008=3773+K+2.
\]
The original defining recurrence, applied to the preceding terms \(x\) and \(y\), says
\[
 a_N=g+\frac{x+y}{g}=g+q.\tag{13}
\]
On the other hand, \(N\geq3775\), so our assumption that the conjectural identity (1) always holds says
\[
 a_N=1+x+y=1+s=1+gq.\tag{14}
\]
Equating (13) and (14) yields
\[
 g+q=1+gq.
\]
Rearrangement gives
\[
 (g-1)(q-1)=0.\tag{15}
\]
But (11) gives \(g-1>0\), and (12) gives \(q-1>0\), contradicting (15).

Thus the first claimed identity cannot hold at every index \(n\geq3775\). In particular, the three identities stated in the conjecture cannot all hold for every such \(n\), so the OEIS A355898 conjecture is false.
